781: What defense is surer against every foe than friendship?
782: The friendship of the wise waxes like the new moon. That of fools wanes like the full moon.
783: Like learning, the friendship of the noble grows more delightful the more you cultivate it.
784: Friendship is not for laughter alone. Its work: to check a friend the moment he goes wrong.
785: Living close and meeting often make no friendship. Only understanding does.
786: The love that lives only in the face's smile is not friendship. True friendship lives deep in the heart's smile.
787: True friendship turns one from evil, helps one walk the good way, and shares one's sorrow in loss.
788: True friendship rushes to help as fast as a hand grabs at a slipping garment in a crowd.
789: Friendship sits enthroned when it can support one at all times and in every circumstance.
790: However much friends praise each other's intimacy, such boasting makes the friendship look small.
791: Good friends never forsake once they love — so nothing is worse than a friendship made without inquiry.
792: Friendship made without repeated inquiry will grieve one to death in the end.
793: Make friendship only after learning a person's character, birth, faults, and all their relations.
794: The friendship of one from a good family who dreads guilt is worth even purchasing.
795: Seek the friendship of those who can make you weep over a fault before you commit it, rebuke you after, and teach you.
796: Even in ruin there is some good: it is the rod that measures the affection of one's kin.
797: It is truly a gain to renounce the friendship of fools.
798: Do not dwell on things that discourage the mind, nor befriend those who forsake you in adversity.
799: The very thought of friends who deserted you when trouble came will burn the mind at death.
800: Keep the friendship of the pure. Give up the friendship of the perverse — even with a parting gift.
801: Intimate friendship is that which cannot be hurt at all by the liberties of long familiarity.
802: The heart of friendship is free familiarity; the wise welcome it gladly.
803: What use is old friendship if a friend disowns what intimacy does?
804: When friends do things unasked through the right of friendship, the wise are pleased at its worth.
805: When friends do what pains, know it comes from ignorance — but also from the strong claims of intimacy.
806: Those who stand within true friendship will not drop old intimacy even in adversity.
807: Those long in the path of affection will not give it up even if their friends bring them ruin.
808: Blessed is the friend who will not listen to tales about friends' faults.
809: The world loves those who never forsake a long-standing, unbroken friendship.
810: Even enemies will love those who have never changed in affection to old friends.
811: Better a shrinking friendship with the envious who "love" you to devour you.
812: What use is the friendship of those who come for gain and go without it?
813: Friends who calculate profit, the wanton out for gain, and thieves are all one kind.
814: Solitude beats the company of those like untrained horses that fling their riders.
815: Better to avoid than to make the evil friendship of the base, who cannot protect even when appointed to.
816: The hatred of the wise is ten million times more profitable than the excessive intimacy of a fool.
817: What comes from enemies is a hundred million times more profitable than what comes from friendship that only laughs.
818: Gradually abandon, without revealing it beforehand, the friendship of those who pretend they cannot do what they can.
819: The friendship of those whose deeds do not match their words will distress one even in dreams.
820: Avoid even the least approach to friendship with those who love you in private and mock you in public.
821: The friendship of the hollow-hearted is a weapon they throw when the moment favors them.
822: The false friend's affection changes like a fickle lover's.
823: However many good books one's foes may master, they cannot become truly loving at heart.
824: Fear the deceitful who smile sweetly with the face but never love with the heart.
825: It is never proper to rely on the words of those who do not love with their heart.
826: Though foes speak as friends, you will taste their meaning at once.
827: As the bending of the bow betokens evil, do not accept the humiliating speech of foes as good.
828: A weapon may hide in the very hands that adore you — and their tears are of the same nature.
829: When foes feign friendship, wear love on the face and let none live in the heart.
830: When foes begin to affect friendship, love them with your looks — and, cherishing no love within, give up even that.
831: Folly is that which makes one incur loss and forego gain.
832: The greatest folly is taking delight in doing what is forbidden.
833: Shamelessness, indifference to what should be sought, harshness, and aversion to everything desirable — these are the fool's qualities.
834: No fool is greater than the one who reads, understands, even teaches — and does not walk by his own teaching.
835: A fool can dig in one lifetime a hell to burn in for seven.
836: If the fool who knows not how to act undertakes a work, he fails — and worse, adorns himself with fetters.
837: A fool's sudden fortune is feasted on by neighbors while his kin go hungry.
838: A fool's possession of anything is like the intoxication of one already giddy.
839: The friendship of fools is sweet to each — parting alone reveals its worth.
840: A fool appearing in an assembly of the learned is like unwashed feet on a bed.
841: Want of wisdom is the greatest of wants. Want of wealth the world does not count a want.
842: When a fool gives cheerfully, it is the receiver's past merit working.
843: The suffering fools inflict on themselves is hardly possible even to foes.
844: Want of wisdom is the vanity that says "we are wise."
845: Fools pretending to know what they never read will raise suspicion even of what they have mastered.
846: Covering the body is folly compared to covering faults — by leaving them.
847: The fool who neglects precious counsel injures himself by his own hand.
848: The fool neither does his duty when advised nor seeks it out — such a soul is a burden to the earth.
849: Teaching a fool only displays one's own folly — the fool still thinks himself wise.
850: Whoever denies what the world holds true will be regarded as a demon on earth.
851: The disease that breeds disunion among all creatures, the wise call hatred.
852: Painful things may be done through disunion; but nothing painful should be done through hatred.
853: Rid yourself of the distressing disease of hatred, and a never-decreasing, imperishable fame is yours.
854: Destroy hatred — the greatest misery — and it yields the greatest delight.
855: Who would think of conquering those who naturally shrink from hatred?
856: Failure and ruin are not far from the one who finds it sweet to excel in hatred.
857: Those full of enmity know only how to work people woe.
858: Shrinking back from hatred yields wealth. Cherishing its increase hastens ruin.
859: No one thinks of hatred when wealth comes. Only those courting ruin nurse it.
860: Hatred causes every calamity. Friendship's delight causes the wealth of virtues.
861: Do not resist the strong; and let no hatred fall upon the weak.
862: How can the unloving, the unsupported, and the strengthless overcome the might of a foe?
863: In the eyes of foes, miserably weak is the timid, ignorant, unsociable, and miserly.
864: Who neither restrains anger nor keeps secrets will be easily conquered by all, at all times and places.
865: A pleasing object to his foes is he who reads no moral works, does no enjoined deed, cares not for reproach, and has no good qualities.
866: Welcome the enmity of those whose anger is blind and whose greed has no measure.
867: It is worth paying for the enmity of those who sabotage their own work.
868: He without good qualities, with many faults, becomes friendless — a help to his foes.
869: No end of lofty delights for the victors whose foes are both ignorant and timid.
870: Fame never comes to the one who has not even fought a foe worth the name.
871: The evil of hatred is not to be desired even in sport.
872: You may incur the hatred of warriors whose ploughs are bows; never that of ministers whose ploughs are words.
873: He who alone incurs the hatred of many is more infatuated than madmen.
874: Great is the ruler whose worthy rule turns foes into friends.
875: He who is alone and helpless, with two foes, should win one of them over as a friendly help.
876: Whatever your misfortune, with a foe neither cling nor break away — act with measure.
877: Relate your suffering not even to ignorant friends; never mention your weakness before foes.
878: The joy of one's foes is destroyed if one guards oneself with right conduct and secures assistance.
879: Cut the thorny tree young. Grown, it breaks the hand that cuts it.
880: Those who do not crush the pride of those who hate them will not survive even to breathe.
881: Shade and water that bring disease give no pleasure. Kin whose ways bring pain give none either.
882: Fear not foes who come openly with the sword. Fear the friendship of those who show you the sole of their foot.
883: Fear internal enmity and guard yourself. Otherwise it will destroy you in an evil hour, as surely as the tool cuts the potter's clay.
884: The secret enmity of the unreformed leads to many evils, breeding disaffection among relations.
885: If internal hatred appears in a royal family, it leads to many a fatal crime.
886: If hatred arises among one's own people, escape from death is hardly possible.
887: A family torn by internal hatred never truly unites, though it may shut together like a casket and lid.
888: A family with internal hatred wears out its strength like filed iron.
889: Though the inward hate be small as a sesame seed, ruin lives inside it.
890: Living with those who disagree with one is like sharing a hut with a cobra.
891: Never underestimate the capable — that matters more than all your guarding.
892: Behaving without respect toward the great invites irremediable evils from them.
893: If you long for ruin, ignore the law and wrong the powerful.
894: The weak doing evil to the strong is beckoning the God of Death to come.
895: Those who have incurred the wrath of a cruel and mighty ruler will not prosper wherever they go.
896: You may survive a forest fire. No one survives disrespecting the great.
897: If a ruler incurs the wrath of the righteous great, what will become of his government with all its wealth?
898: If the hill-like great resolve on destruction, those who seemed everlasting will be uprooted from the earth.
899: Even kings fall from their height and perish in that flame.
900: Though in possession of numerous auxiliaries, they perish who are exposed to the wrath of the noble whose penance is boundless.
901: Those consumed by desire for their wives lose the excellence of virtue — the very excellence the ambitious cannot afford to lose.
902: The wealth of one lost in his wife's allure ends in shame for him and all around.
903: The frailty that stoops to a wife's every wish always shames her husband among the good.
904: Nothing the henpecked undertake is ever praised.
905: He that fears his wife will always be afraid of doing good deeds even to the good.
906: The wife-fearing lack manliness, though they flourish like gods.
907: A bashful woman is worth more than a shameless man lost in lust.
908: Those who yield to their wives' wishes will neither relieve friends' wants nor perform virtuous deeds.
909: From those who obey their wives' commands expect neither virtue, nor wealth, nor even pleasure.
910: The folly of being wife-led is never found in the thoughtful and the self-possessed.
